explanations: terra: Breaking covenant and cutting what God ordered joined gives a second direct reversal of the section’s connected word, connected people, and continuous plant cover.

luna: Adam and his wife are told to dwell together in the Garden; the section's dictionary form of miskin derives from s-k-n, settling toward a beloved, and this ayah gives that rest a domestic scene.

luna: The covenantal command groups kindness to parents, relatives, orphans, and needy people, the same move from descent to wider care that the section traces. | terra: The covenant places kindness to parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy together, the same movement from lineage to restorative care that the section hears across surah 90.
terra: When Abraham asks that leadership extend to his offspring, God excludes wrongdoers from the covenant; biological descent is acknowledged but bounded by moral qualification.
luna: Abraham asks God to make this town secure and provide its people with fruits, joining the section's town, sheltering neighbors, and relief from hunger.
luna: Abraham asks that he, his son, and their descendants be made submitting community; lineage becomes a chain of shared faith like the section's tawāṣī.

luna: The section's counsel-as-connection has a generational form here: Abraham and Jacob transmit their faith to their sons through waṣṣā, a testament. | terra: Abraham and Jacob وَصَّىٰ their sons with faith, making counsel a word carried through a family line rather than a merely private instruction.
luna: The sons answer their father's deathbed question by naming the God of their fathers; this neighbor completes 2:132's transmission of faith down the family line.

luna: This account of righteousness combines kin, orphan, needy, freeing a neck (fī al-riqāb), and patience, closely joining the section's bodily and communal scenes. | terra: Righteousness gives cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, and the needy, frees necks, keeps commitments, and remains patient; it assembles nearly the whole social ascent of 90:13–17.

luna: The source section says waṣiyya (bequest, from root w-ṣ-y) is speech joined across people; this ayah directs a bequest to parents and near kin at death. | terra: الْوَصِيَّةُ is prescribed for parents and near relatives, concretely realizing the section’s dictionary image of a linked word that reaches across kinship.

luna: The section's near orphan and dust-covered poor reappear in the giving order: parents, near kin, orphans, and the needy receive wealth. | terra: Spending proceeds to parents, near kin, orphans, and the needy, showing how the biological relation of وَالِدَيْنِ widens into provision for those whose relations have failed.

luna: After asking about orphans, the ayah says that mixing lives with theirs makes them your brothers; it reverses the section's orphan as lineage cut off into chosen kinship. | terra: The instruction about orphans says that setting their affairs right is best and that, if believers mix with them, they are their brothers; isolated children are deliberately rejoined to a household.

luna: This ayah makes the child's nursing a shared parental responsibility, requires mutual consent and consultation, and forbids harming a mother through her child. | terra: Mothers nurse, the father provides, and neither parent may be harmed through the child; the ayah turns biological parenthood into a sustained network of care.
luna: A man nearing death must provide a bequest for his wife; this joins the section's waṣiyya (connected speech) to care for a surviving family member.

luna: God forms people in wombs as He wills; this supplies a direct but general parallel to the section's hidden completion of the child before birth. | terra: God forms people in the wombs as He wills; this is the direct Quranic setting for the section’s خ ل ق sense of a completed bodily form within the mother.
luna: God chooses Adam, Noah, Abraham's family, and Imran's family, giving the section's parentage and descent a prophetic lineage.
luna: The chosen line is described as descendants of one another; this is a direct formulation of lineage continuing through generations.
terra: Mary’s mother speaks when she has delivered her child, and God knows best what she delivered; the ayah stages الولادة itself and the parent’s first relation to the newborn.

luna: Zechariah asks God for good offspring, repeating the section's concern with descendants as a gift. | terra: Zechariah asks God for good offspring, expressing lineage as a prayed-for gift that should carry goodness forward.
luna: The angel announces Yahya, completing Zechariah's prayer for offspring in 3:38.

luna: Zechariah names old age and his wife's barrenness; the promised birth overturns the section's dictionary image of a woman whose children do not survive. | terra: Zechariah names his old age and his wife’s barrenness when promised a son, directly staging the bodily threat that a family line will end.

luna: God joins hearts that had been enemies until they become brothers; this is a direct communal counterpart to the section's movement from severed kinship to a joined, merciful people. | terra: God joins formerly hostile hearts so that people become brothers while all hold fast together, a direct nonlexical parallel to separate lives becoming one continuous cover.

luna: The Prophet's gentleness keeps people from dispersing, and he is told to pardon and consult them; this specifies mercy as a force that holds a community together. | terra: Divine mercy makes the Prophet gentle; harshness would make people disperse from around him, so pardon and consultation visibly turn possible scattering into community.

luna: This ayah puts al-arham (kinship ties) beside raqiban (a watcher), exactly the womb-to-relatives and raqaba-to-oversight branches the section develops. | terra: Humanity spreads from one soul and its mate; the command to guard الْأَرْحَامَ appears with God as رَقِيبًا, bringing shared womb, kinship, descendants, and the section’s secondary رق ب sense into one ayah.

luna: The command to return orphans' property and not consume it joins the section's fatherless child to concrete protection by the surrounding community. | terra: The command to return orphans’ property and not consume it protects the parentless child from a second severance at the hands of the surrounding community.
luna: The ayah specifically warns guardians about justice to orphan girls, extending the section's orphan image to vulnerable kin whose care is entrusted to others.

luna: Orphans are to be tested until marriageable and then given their property; this follows the section's severed lineage into protection as a child grows up. | terra: Guardians test the orphans until maturity and release their property when they آنَسْتُمْ sound judgment; the root of familiarity or perception occurs precisely in care for the parentless child.

luna: The ayah assigns inheritance shares to men and women from parents and near kin, tying succession after death to the section's line of offspring and relatives. | terra: Men and women alike receive assigned shares from what parents and near relatives leave, giving legal continuity to lineage after death.

luna: At inheritance division, relatives, orphans, and needy people who are present must receive provision; the estate becomes a means of care for the section's vulnerable figures. | terra: When relatives, orphans, and the needy attend an inheritance division, they too must be provided for and addressed kindly; inherited wealth is made to widen care beyond the direct heirs.
luna: The warning to fear leaving weak offspring and to speak rightly connects adult decisions to the children who may be left without protection.

luna: Consuming orphan property is described as eating fire; this is the sharp opposite of the section's feeding and mercy toward the orphan. | terra: Those who consume orphans’ wealth are described as taking fire into themselves, the severe opposite of feeding and protecting a child cut off from a father.
luna: The ayah specifies children and parents as heirs, making the section's continuing lineage concrete in the distribution of a parent's estate.
luna: This inheritance law names spouses, children, and siblings; it shows family ties persisting as claims after death, as the section's lineage image implies.
luna: The prohibited kin categories include mothers who bore you and sisters through nursing; the ayah grounds family closeness in birth and shared nurture.

luna: This ayah gathers parents, kin, orphan, poor, near neighbor, and companion by one's side, then condemns the boastful; it directly mirrors the section's circle of care and its rich boaster's opposite. | terra: Parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, near and distant neighbors, the companion at one’s side, and those under one’s hand form an expanding ring of nearness opposed to boastful pride.

luna: For accidental killing, this ayah requires freeing a believing neck and compensation to the victim's family unless waived; it links release, severed life, kin, and mercy. | terra: Accidental killing is answered by freeing a believing neck and compensation delivered to the victim’s family, joining a life cut off, surviving kin, and emancipation as repair.
luna: Justice must stand even against parents and near relatives; the section's qarāba (kinship) is a bond, but not a license to abandon justice.

luna: The command to cooperate in righteousness and piety gives the section's mutual connection a practical communal form. | terra: The command to cooperate in righteousness and reverence gives a direct ethical form to people supporting one another rather than remaining separate.

luna: Among the expiations for broken oaths are feeding needy people or freeing a neck, repeating the section's concrete acts of relief. | terra: Expiation for a broken oath includes feeding the needy or freeing a neck, bringing oath, provision, and تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ together as surah 90 does.
terra: Those who believe without clothing faith in wrongdoing receive الْأَمْنُ and guidance, explicitly deriving security from the same root as آمَنُوا.
luna: Each person comes alone, leaving wealth and intercessors behind; this directly contrasts the section's isolated orphan and its turn toward companions.
terra: Humanity is produced from one soul and given a place of settlement and a place of deposit, an indirect parallel to one origin unfolding into embodied and social locations.
luna: Those who kill their children foolishly and forbid God's provision enact a stark severing of the line the section traces from birth.
terra: The same counsel sequence commands kindness to parents and forbids killing children because of poverty, protecting both ends of lineage where want could sever them.

luna: Here yatim (orphan), dhā qurba (near kin), and waṣṣākum (He enjoined you) meet in one command, as in the section's linked image of kinship, orphan care, and mutual counsel. | terra: The ayah protects the orphan’s property, requires justice even toward ذَا قُرْبَىٰ, and closes with وَصَّاكُم, explicitly joining orphanhood, nearness, and binding counsel.
luna: The same command to dwell in the Garden is addressed to Adam and his wife, repeating the section's s-k-n link between rest and companionship.
luna: Pharaoh promises successful magicians a place among the near ones; this repeated q-r-b wording makes nearness a worldly favor, unlike the section's faith-based closeness.
luna: The Messenger removes burdens and shackles from people; this is a direct reversal of the section's bound neck and its act of freeing a raqaba.

luna: The spouses seek repose in one another (root s-k-n), while the woman carries a light burden that grows heavy; this joins the section's miskin root and pregnancy image. | terra: A single soul finds repose in its mate, who then bears first a light and then a heavy pregnancy and prays for a sound child; dwelling, gestation, and offspring form one continuous scene.

luna: The share of public spoils is assigned to the Messenger, near kin, orphans, needy, and travelers, linking kin descent to provision for the vulnerable. | terra: A share of acquired wealth is assigned to near kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler, repeating the section’s widening order of provision.

luna: God joins believers' hearts when no wealth could have united them; this makes the section's joining of separate people into a community concrete. | terra: God unites believers’ hearts in a bond that all the earth’s wealth could not purchase, clarifying why wealth cannot produce the nearness that faith produces.
terra: Those who migrate and strive and those who shelter and help them become protecting allies of one another, a concrete community formed by refuge rather than common birth.
terra: The migrants and those who shelter and help are named true believers and promised forgiveness and generous provision, confirming the faith-bond enacted in 8:72.
terra: Blood relatives are declared nearer to one another while later believers still belong to the faithful community, defining the relationship between womb-nearness and chosen fellowship.
terra: Even an enemy seeking protection must be granted refuge and escorted to safety, realizing the section’s companion and neighbor senses as protection that removes fear.
luna: Believers are told not to take fathers and brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief; blood ties have a faith boundary, like the section's turn from descent to belief.
terra: Fathers, sons, brothers, spouses, clan, wealth, trade, and homes become a danger when loved above God and His cause; the whole network of nearness is retained but morally bounded.
luna: After the believers are shaken in battle, God sends tranquility upon them; this directly illustrates faith's removal of fear.
terra: The Prophet tells his cave companion not to grieve because God is with them, and tranquility descends; companionship here visibly performs the section’s protection and removal of fear.
luna: Zakat recipients include the poor, needy, and those in the necks (fī al-riqāb); the ayah gathers the section's poverty and emancipation images.

luna: Believing men and women are allies of one another and command good; it gives the section's connected, merciful community a wider social form. | terra: Believing men and women are protecting allies who enjoin right and receive God’s mercy; faith, reciprocal guidance, protection, and mercy become one community.
luna: The ayah bars prayer for forgiveness for even close polytheist kin; it makes faith a specific boundary within the section's kinship bond.

luna: Sarah receives the announcement of Isaac despite her age, a birth reversal of the section's lexicon for a woman without living children. | terra: Sarah receives news of Isaac and, after Isaac, Jacob, making childbirth also the promise of a grandchild who remains after the first generation.
luna: Sarah names herself an old barren woman; this completes the childbirth surprise begun in 11:71.
luna: The visitors answer with God's decree and mercy, completing the announcement to the parents in 11:71-72.
luna: The disbelievers are described with fetters around their necks, the opposite of the section's freeing a bound neck.

luna: God knows what each female carries and what wombs diminish or increase, a direct formulation of the section's hidden pregnancy and approaching birth. | terra: God knows what every female carries and what wombs diminish or increase, grounding the section’s signs of approaching birth in hidden gestation and exact measure.

luna: The section defines mutual counsel as joining one thing to another; this ayah praises those who join what God commanded to be joined, including kin ties. | terra: Those praised connect what God commanded to be connected and fear their Lord, a direct thematic expression of the section’s movement from solitary rupture to maintained bonds.
luna: This neighbor adds the section's patience and giving: those who join bonds endure patiently, pray, spend from provision, and repel evil with good.

luna: The joining culminates in the presence of righteous parents, spouses, and descendants together in the Garden, completing the family and communal bond of 13:21. | terra: The righteous enter lasting gardens together with righteous parents, spouses, and descendants, so kinship and moral formation culminate in a gathered household.
terra: Those condemned sever what God commanded to be joined, providing the exact reversal of the section’s تواصي as connection.
terra: A good word is a good tree with firm root and raised branches, joining the section’s connected speech to living growth in a single image.
terra: The tree continually gives fruit by its Lord’s leave, completing 14:24’s account of how a rooted word persists and nourishes beyond its first speaker.
luna: Abraham asks for a secure town and protection for himself and his sons, joining residence, safety, and descendants as the section does through city, family, and faith.

luna: Abraham settles some of his offspring in the uncultivated valley by the Sacred House and asks that hearts incline to them and provision come; lineage and place become a community. | terra: Abraham settles some of his offspring in an uncultivated valley, asks that they establish prayer, and asks for human hearts and provision to draw toward them; barren ground, lineage, dwelling, and communal attachment meet in one scene.
terra: Abraham praises God for granting Ishmael and Isaac in old age, a fulfilled lineage after bodily delay.

luna: Abraham asks that he and his descendants keep prayer, tying offspring to shared faith and practice. | terra: Abraham asks that he and some of his descendants establish prayer, carrying religious practice down the family line opened in 14:39.
luna: Abraham asks how a child can be announced to him in old age, a direct birth reversal of childlessness.
luna: The angels reaffirm the good news, completing Abraham's question about the announced child.
luna: Abraham says only the astray despair of God's mercy; this neighbor completes the promise to elderly parents with the section's mercy theme.

luna: The father darkens at news of a daughter and considers hiding her; the ayah shows a family refusing the bond at birth. | terra: The father’s face darkens at news of a daughter, showing parenthood received as shame rather than the entrusted bond developed by the section.

luna: He debates keeping the girl in humiliation or burying her in dust; this directly reverses the section's birth and its image of the poor fallen into dust. | terra: Hiding from people and considering burying the daughter turns estrangement into lethal severance, completing 16:58’s reversal of parental mercy.

luna: The ayah names spouses, children, and grandchildren as God's provision, a direct statement of the lineage continuing from the section's walid and walad. | terra: God makes spouses, children, and grandchildren and provides good things, laying out the widening household produced by birth across two generations.

luna: People emerge from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then receive hearing, sight, and hearts; birth opens into dependence and responsibility. | terra: God brings people from their mothers’ wombs knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, connecting birth to the section’s concern with what a human sees.
luna: Homes are made a sakan (resting place); this Qur'anic sense of the section's miskin root links shelter to the family home.

luna: God commands giving to relatives, directly extending the section's qarāba (kinship) from a dictionary sense into a Qur'anic duty. | terra: Justice and excellence culminate in giving to near kin, a concise command that turns the section’s root of nearness into social mercy.
terra: This ayah requires gentle speech and honor when one or both parents reach old age; 17:24 then turns that long care into the child’s prayer for mercy.

luna: The section turns the womb's kinship into mercy between generations; the prayer asks God to show parents mercy as they raised the speaker when small. | terra: The child asks God to show the parents mercy as they raised the child when small, returning رَحْمَة to the parent-child relation from which the section’s womb imagery begins.

luna: The command to give the relative, poor person, and traveler their due makes the section's near kin and dust-covered poor recipients of actual provision. | terra: The relative receives a due alongside the needy and traveler, translating nearness into provision for both kin and socially exposed people.
luna: The hand chained to the neck is an image of withholding wealth; the ayah warns against stinginess, reversing the section's freeing of a neck and feeding the needy.

luna: The command not to kill children from fear of poverty directly reverses the section's threatened lineage and the needy child's vulnerability. | terra: Killing children for fear of poverty is forbidden because God provides for parent and child, the starkest deliberate severing of lineage at the point where need should summon care.

luna: The command not to approach an orphan's property until maturity protects the fatherless child through the period when the section's lineage would otherwise be interrupted. | terra: The orphan’s property may be approached only for improvement until maturity, sustaining the child through the period opened by paternal loss.

luna: The rich garden-owner boasts of wealth and children; his ṣāḥib (companion) answers him, contrasting the section's boastful man with a companion who counsels him. | terra: A man boasts to his companion of greater wealth and a stronger following; 18:37 turns that companionship into correction by recalling his created origin.
luna: The wealthy man enters his garden wronging himself, turning the section's connected plant image into private possession and self-regard.
luna: He doubts the Hour and assumes his garden will endure, the opposite of the section's dependence on faith, patience, and care for vulnerable people.

luna: His companion answers that God created him from dust and then a drop; birth and companionship challenge wealth as the measure of a person. | terra: The garden owner’s companion answers his boast by recalling that he was created from dust and then a drop, joining companionship to the section’s earthen and generative origins.
luna: The garden's fruit is ruined and its owner wrings his hands, reversing the section's plant growth and the boast that possessions endure.
luna: He has no group to help him against God, the isolated end of a man whose section-like wealth and descendants did not make a merciful community.
luna: Protection and true authority belong to God, completing the garden owner's loss of human support in 18:43.
terra: Worldly life is vegetation that flourishes with rain and then becomes scattered debris, a temporal reversal of the section’s continuous green cover.
terra: Wealth and children are adornment, while lasting good deeds are better; after 18:45’s scattered vegetation, the ayah distinguishes inherited display from what truly remains.
terra: A wall protects treasure for two orphan boys until maturity because their father was righteous; a dead parent’s care is carried forward by God and a compassionate stranger.
luna: Zechariah describes his weakened bones and gray hair; this ayah supplies the old age that makes his successor prayer in 19:5 urgent.

luna: Zechariah fears that his family line will have no successor and asks for an heir; this is the section's concern with descendants who remain after a man. | terra: Zechariah fears what will follow him while his wife is barren and asks for an heir, combining succession with the possibility that lineage will stop.

luna: The requested son is to inherit Zechariah and the family of Jacob; this neighbor specifies the successor relation behind the preceding plea. | terra: The requested child will inherit from Zechariah and Jacob’s house, specifying the continuing عقب sought in 19:5.

luna: The answer is the promised Yahya, a child born despite the parents' circumstances, completing the successor prayer in 19:5-6. | terra: The promise of Yahya answers the threatened break in 19:5–6 with a named child and renewed descent.
luna: Zechariah names his old age and his wife's barrenness; the ayah makes the threatened birth and succession explicit.
luna: God answers that creating Yahya is easy; the sign completes the reversal of the barrenness described in 19:8.

luna: Mary conceives and withdraws with the child, extending the section's lineage image to a solitary pregnancy. | terra: Mary conceives Jesus and withdraws with him to a distant place, presenting the hidden carrying that precedes the section’s act of birth.

luna: Mary's labor pains bring her to a palm trunk; this is a direct bodily scene of imminent delivery. | terra: Labor pains drive Mary to the palm trunk, making the hardship of delivery concrete and answering the section’s conjunction of birth with human كبد.
luna: The voice beneath Mary reassures her during labor and points to a stream, completing the birth scene of 19:23 with relief.
luna: The instruction to shake the palm so fresh dates fall gives Mary food immediately after labor, a concrete provision around childbirth.
luna: Mary is told to eat, drink, and be comforted after birth; this completes the bodily and emotional care around the delivery.
terra: Ishmael commands his household to prayer and almsgiving, another instance of guidance carried through the family relation.
luna: The wealthy claimant is told that his possessions will be inherited and that he will come alone; this directly answers the section's boaster, wealth, descendants, and solitude.
luna: Everyone comes to God individually on the Day of Resurrection, a boundary to the section's collective companionship.
terra: The infant Moses is placed in a chest and cast into the river, yet divine love and watchful care accompany him; a child exposed to severance remains held within protection.
terra: Moses’s sister leads others to a caregiver and he is returned to his mother so that she will not grieve, a compressed repeated formulation of kinship repaired after separation.
terra: The Prophet is told to command his family to prayer and persist in it, pairing household guidance with the patience that the section’s believers exchange.

luna: Zechariah asks not to be left without an heir; the section's dictionary sense of a successor who remains after a man is stated as a prayer. | terra: Zechariah asks not to be left alone without an heir, giving personal voice to the section’s image of solitary severance from continuing offspring.

luna: God responds by granting Yahya and making Zechariah's wife fit for childbirth, reversing the childlessness that threatened the line in 21:89. | terra: God answers Zechariah, makes his wife fit, and describes the family hastening together in good works with hope and fear; restored lineage becomes a bound worshipping household.

luna: The ayah describes creation from drop to clot to formed or unformed lump, placement in wombs, and emergence as infants: a full bodily arc behind the section's birth image. | terra: The ayah places human gestation and birth beside dead earth stirring and growing plants, directly joining the section’s womb-made body to its image of separate growth becoming living cover.

luna: Humanity's creation begins from an extract of clay, carrying the section's parent-and-child image back to the origin of human bodies. | terra: Human creation begins from an extract of clay, supplying the earthen origin before 23:13 places the next generative stage in a secure resting place.

luna: The drop is placed in a secure resting place; this gives the section's womb-as-house-and-vessel an exact Qur'anic scene. | terra: The human is placed as a drop in a secure resting place, locating created lineage within the protected bodily container described in the section as the child’s house.

luna: The successive clot, lump, bones, and flesh make the section's otherwise hidden formation in the womb visible. | terra: Successive embryonic forms culminate in another creation, directly expanding the section’s خ ل ق sense from formed part to completed human life.

luna: On the Day the Trumpet is blown, there are no family ties among them; this marks a boundary to the lineage bond the section traces. | terra: At the trumpet there are no lineage ties between people and no mutual questioning, an eschatological boundary on the earthly continuity named by parent, child, and descendants.

luna: The ayah names kin, poor, and emigrants while urging pardon and continued giving; it turns closeness into mercy toward vulnerable people. | terra: People of means must not stop giving to relatives, the needy, and migrants but should pardon and overlook, joining provision to the mercy that preserves damaged relations.

luna: The section's insan dictionary branch is familiarity without estrangement; here tasta'nisū means seeking familiarity before entering another household, beside greeting its people. | terra: Believers may not enter others’ homes until تَسْتَأْنِسُوا and greet their people, turning non-estrangement into a concrete ethic of neighboring presence.
luna: This neighbor sets the boundary for the household visit in 24:27: if no one is there, do not enter without permission.
luna: The ayah orders help for enslaved people seeking a freedom contract and aid from God's provision, a concrete social form of releasing the bound neck.
terra: God promises believing doers of good that fear will be exchanged for security, unfolding the section’s root definition of faith as fear’s departure at communal scale.

luna: Humanity is made from water and given blood kinship and marriage ties; this directly joins bodily origin to the social bonds the section traces. | terra: The human made from water is given both blood lineage and marriage affinity, directly naming the two relations by which birth extends into a connected human family.

luna: The prayer for spouses and offspring who are a comfort to the eyes presents family closeness as a desired good, echoing the section's companion and descendant images. | terra: The servants of God ask that spouses and offspring become comfort to their eyes and that they become examples for the God-conscious, joining family joy to communal moral leadership.
luna: Pharaoh offers the successful magicians a place among the muqarrabīn; nearness is presented as worldly favor, unlike the section's faith-shaped nearness to God.
terra: The Day when neither wealth nor children benefit marks the limit of both possessions as a bond that can save.
luna: The command to warn one's nearest kin takes qarāba as a concrete circle of address, matching the section's movement from close family outward.

terra: Moses’s mother is told to nurse him, cast him into the river when afraid, and trust the promise that he will be returned; maternal care is stretched across an apparent severing without being broken.
terra: Moses’s mother is left with an emptied heart and nearly reveals him until God strengthens it, giving the section’s threatened parent-child rupture an inward form.
terra: The mother tells Moses’s sister to follow him, so kinship continues to watch over the separated infant from a distance.
terra: After the infant refuses other nursing women, his sister offers a household that will care sincerely for him, making the biological family the means of protection even before recognition.
terra: God restores Moses to his mother so that her eye may be comforted and she may not grieve, completing the passage’s movement from forced separation to renewed maternal security.
luna: People fear being snatched from their land if they follow guidance, while God has established a secure sanctuary and provision; this connects the section's town and neighboring life to safety.
luna: Qarun is arrogant among his people because of vast wealth, a specific contrast to the section's generosity toward the poor.
luna: His people tell him to do good as God has done good to him and not seek corruption; this states the social use of wealth that the section asks for.
luna: Qarun claims his wealth came from his own knowledge, opposing the section's account of human dependence and mutual care.
luna: Qarun and his house are swallowed and no group can help him; wealth and household fail to provide the companionship the section values.
luna: The onlookers learn that provision is not proof of favor, completing Qarun's fall and the section's challenge to wealth-based honor.

luna: The command to treat parents well is bounded when they press their child toward idolatry; the family tie remains, but faith sets a limit, as in the section's turn from lineage to belief. | terra: وَصَّيْنَا الْإِنسَانَ بِوَالِدَيْهِ makes divine counsel itself carry the bond between the human and both parents, while also setting a boundary when they press for idolatry.
terra: Isaac and Jacob are granted to Abraham and prophethood and scripture are placed among his descendants, showing lineage carrying a word and vocation onward.
luna: God made the sanctuary secure while people around it were seized; this connects the section's town and neighbor image to safety within a shared place.
terra: Creation from dust is followed by humans spreading abroad, so the solitary material origin becomes a dispersed and multiplying human population.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of miskin uses the root s-k-n for what the heart settles toward; here spouses are made so each may find repose in the other, alongside affection and mercy. | terra: Spouses are created so that one may لِتَسْكُنُوا إِلَيْهَا, with affection and mercy between them; this states the section’s secondary sense of مسكين’s root as resting in a beloved and joins it to رحم.

luna: The command to give relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due is the ethical form of the section's closeness and care. | terra: Giving relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due is named as the course that seeks God’s face, so proximity becomes an enacted bond rather than mere descent.
terra: Luqman’s tender address to his son begins a sustained act of counsel, showing how a linked word first passes within a parent-child relation.

luna: The source section begins with walid (parent) and walada (to give birth); here the mother carries her child through weakness upon weakness and nurses him, grounding the parent-child bond in bodily cost. | terra: The counsel concerning parents recalls a mother carrying in weakness upon weakness and weaning the child, making parental bond and the bodily cost of lineage inseparable.

luna: Even when parents urge idolatry, the child must not obey, yet must accompany them kindly; it marks faith as the boundary of descent while preserving mercy. | terra: After the mother’s hardship in 31:14, the child must not obey parental idolatry but must accompany both parents honorably in this world; companionship preserves care without erasing moral limits.
terra: Luqman tells his son that even a mustard-seed deed hidden in rock will be brought forth by God, answering the section’s question whether anyone sees before 31:17 commands patience.
terra: Luqman tells his son to establish prayer, enjoin right, forbid wrong, and be patient, making parental counsel the training ground for the patience later exchanged within a believing community.
luna: God alone knows what is in wombs; the ayah makes explicit the hidden pregnancy behind the section's visible signs of approaching birth.
terra: Human progeny is made from an extract of humble fluid, directly naming the continuation of the line through bodily generation.
terra: God proportions the human and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, connecting formed gestational life to the perceiving person addressed in surah 90.

luna: The ayah says adopted sons are not one's actual sons, distinguishing social naming from the descent through a womb that the section develops. | terra: The ayah denies that a wife called “mother” becomes a mother or that an adopted son becomes a biological son, guarding the meanings of womb, birth, and lineage on which the section depends.

luna: Children are to be called by their fathers, which makes the section's father-based lineage explicit as a recognized tie. | terra: Calling adopted children by their fathers preserves actual lineage, while those whose fathers are unknown become brothers in faith and close associates; biological and chosen bonds are carefully joined.

luna: The ayah says blood relatives are closer to one another than other believers, setting inherited kinship beside the faith-based community of the section. | terra: The Prophet is nearer to believers and his wives are their mothers, yet blood relatives remain nearer by divine ordinance; communal and genealogical kinship are held together without confusion.
luna: The section's dictionary branch of uns is familiarity; this ayah uses musta'nisīn for guests lingering in conversation and sets a boundary for entering the Prophet's household.

luna: The deniers claim that greater wealth and children protect them; this is the precise boast the section rebukes through its rich spender and its warning that offspring do not bring nearness. | terra: The prosperous claim that greater wealth and more children protect them from punishment; 34:37 answers that neither possession creates nearness to God.
luna: The next ayah says provision expands or contracts by God's will, completing the reply to the wealthy people's claim in 34:35.

luna: The section explicitly asks whether wealth and children bind people to God; this ayah says amwāl (wealth) and awlād (children) do not bring nearness, while faith and good action do. | terra: Wealth and children do not bring people near to God; faith and good action do, directly correcting inherited or possessed nearness with the section’s final bond of belief and deed.

luna: People are created from dust and then a drop, and females carry and deliver only with God's knowledge; this joins dust, descent, and pregnancy in one ayah. | terra: Creation from dust and a drop becomes paired life, pregnancy, and birth, all under divine knowledge; it gathers the section’s soil, lineage, womb, and visible or hidden gestation.
luna: Fetters reach the disbelievers' chins and hold their heads raised; this is a specific reversal of releasing the neck.

luna: After Noah's deliverance, his offspring are made the survivors; the ayah states lineage continuing beyond the father. | terra: Noah’s descendants are made the survivors, a large-scale instance of عقب as children remaining after catastrophe.

luna: Abraham asks for a righteous child, directly voicing the desire for lineage to continue. | terra: Abraham asks his Lord to grant him a righteous child, placing the continuation of descent within prayer and moral hope.

luna: The answer announces a forbearing boy, completing Abraham's prayer for offspring in 37:100. | terra: The good news of a forbearing boy answers 37:100 and supplies the child who later grows into the patient companion of his father in 37:102.

luna: The son has grown to work alongside his father; this is the section's dictionary branch of the son who becomes his father's companion. | terra: When Abraham’s son reaches the age of working beside him, father and son deliberate over the sacrifice and the son promises patience; grown companionship, filial counsel, and hardship meet here.
luna: Father and son submit together to the commanded sacrifice, bringing the threatened severing of descent into the very scene of their companionship.
luna: A great ransom replaces the son; this neighbor completes the threatened lineage break with deliverance.

luna: The word atrāb again means peers of equal age, preserving the section's secondary tirb sense in another Qur'anic description of company. | terra: The companions kept near in the garden are أَتْرَابٌ, another direct use of the section’s soil-root in its peer and age-mate sense.
luna: The disbelievers claim their idols bring them closer to God; this contrasts the section's true closeness through faith and compassionate action with a false means of approach.

luna: God creates people in their mothers' wombs through successive formations in three darknesses, a direct image of the body's hidden preparation for birth. | terra: Creation after creation in three darknesses inside mothers’ wombs gives the hidden bodily sequence behind وَوَالِدٍ وَمَا وَلَدَ.
terra: The angels ask that believers be admitted with the righteous among their parents, spouses, and descendants, making mercy the force that reunites generations.

luna: The ayah follows a human from dust through a drop and clot to infant, adulthood, and old age, linking birth to the full lineage-bearing life. | terra: Creation moves from dust and a drop through a clot to emergence as a child, maturity, old age, and death; the full lineage-bearing life is shown as successive vulnerable stages.
luna: The condemned are dragged with shackles around their necks, a direct contrary scene to freeing the neck in the section.
luna: Repelling evil with what is better can turn an enemy into an intimate friend; this is a specific reversal from separation to the section's joined community.
luna: The next ayah says this change is granted to the patient, completing the enemy-to-friend reversal with the section's counsel to patience.
terra: No female conceives or gives birth without God’s knowledge, setting the section’s outward signs of pregnancy against the divine knowledge that encompasses the whole event.
luna: The ayah names affection toward near kin as a requested reward; the referent of the phrase is debated, but its kinship link is explicit.

luna: God gives daughters or sons as offspring, making descent a gift rather than a human guarantee. | terra: God grants daughters to some and sons to others, presenting offspring as a gift rather than the possession implied by human boasting.

luna: God may give both sexes or make whom He wills barren, a direct boundary on the lineage continuation named in the section. | terra: God joins sons and daughters for some and makes others barren, marking both continuation and the threatened break in lineage developed through the section’s dictionary senses.

luna: Abraham's declaration is made a lasting word among his descendants; this directly joins counsel and belief across generations. | terra: Abraham makes the word enduring فِي عَقِبِهِ, joining the section’s secondary sense of عقب as descendants who remain after a man to its image of speech passed onward.
luna: Intimate friends become enemies on that Day except the Godwary; the section's companion and mercy roots find their boundary in faith.

luna: The section links parents, birth, and the mother's bodily labor; this ayah joins kindness to parents with carrying and delivering a child in hardship, then names the period of pregnancy and weaning. | terra: وَصَّيْنَا links counsel to parents while the mother carries and delivers in hardship, the Quranic meeting of the section’s birth oath, human كبد, and connected speech.
terra: Following the mother’s hardship in 46:15, the grown child asks that offspring be made righteous and is accepted among the garden’s companions; care passes forward through generations.

luna: A child rebukes parents who call him to faith despite their care; this is the opposite of gratitude for parental labor in the section and in 46:15. | terra: After 46:15–16 trace a mother’s hardship and a grateful child’s prayer for descendants, this child says contemptuously to both parents and rejects their warning, staging filial connection broken from within.

luna: The section traces birth's threatened interruption and asks for a community bound by mercy; this ayah names cutting al-arham (womb ties) as social corruption. | terra: تُقَطِّعُوا أَرْحَامَكُمْ makes severed womb-relations the social consequence of corruption, the explicit opposite of mercy gathering people as if from one womb.

luna: God sends sakīna into believers' hearts to increase their faith; the section describes faith as calm and the departure of fear. | terra: Tranquility descends into believers’ hearts and increases faith, closely matching the section’s definition of security as the soul becoming calm.
luna: At the pledge under the tree, God sends tranquility into believers' hearts; this is another communal instance of faith settling fear.
luna: God sends tranquility on the Messenger and believers and binds them to piety, joining faith and calm in a community.

luna: The section joins plant growth to people who show mercy among themselves; this ayah calls believers merciful among themselves and likens their mutual strengthening to a crop sending out a shoot. | terra: The believers are رُحَمَاءُ بَيْنَهُمْ and also a crop whose shoots strengthen one another, exactly fusing the section’s communal mercy with its connected-plant sense of تَوَاصَوْا.
terra: Believers are commanded to reconcile two fighting groups with justice, supplying the active repair that allows 49:10 to call all believers brothers.

luna: Believers are called brothers and told to reconcile; it states the section's movement from isolated people to a bound community. | terra: Believers are brothers, so fractured relations must be repaired and God feared so that mercy may be received; the ayah states the social kinship produced by faith.

luna: Humanity is made peoples and tribes to know one another, while honor is measured by piety; descent becomes a path to recognition rather than rank. | terra: Creation from male and female becomes peoples and tribes so that humans may know one another, expanding birth into social familiarity rather than estrangement.
luna: The ayah says God is nearer than the jugular vein; it gives the section's q-r-b theme a bodily image while making nearness more than human kinship.
luna: The righteous keep a known right in their wealth for the asker and deprived, making the section's care for the poor a recurring social obligation.
luna: The visitors give Abraham news of a knowledgeable son, repeating the unexpected birth that answers a childless household.

luna: Sarah calls herself an old barren woman; the promised child reverses the section's image of a woman whose child does not live. | terra: Abraham’s wife strikes her face and calls herself old and barren, voicing the bodily impossibility against which promised birth renews lineage.
luna: The visitors confirm that God has decreed the birth, completing Sarah's question in 51:29.

luna: The ayah asks whether deniers across generations advised one another to reject truth; its ironic use of tawāṣaw is the reverse of the section's counsel in patience and mercy. | terra: أَتَوَاصَوْا بِهِ asks whether rejecting generations passed their falsehood to one another, turning the section’s mutually sustaining counsel into a transmitted bond of rebellion.

luna: Believing descendants are joined to their parents in the Garden; lineage is preserved through faith, matching the section's shift from birth to a believing community. | terra: Believing descendants are joined to believing parents without diminishing anyone’s deeds, giving the section’s threatened lineage an image of final reunion through faith.
terra: God knows humans both when they arise from earth and when they are embryos in their mothers’ wombs, joining the section’s soil and gestational images under one knowledge.

luna: The ayah says God creates the two sexes, male and female, a direct account of the offspring arising from the section's birth image. | terra: God creates the two sexes, male and female, locating the paired possibility from which parents and descendants arise.

luna: The creation of male and female is traced to an emitted drop, specifying the origin behind 53:45. | terra: The pair in 53:45 comes from a drop when emitted, specifying the bodily origin of the generative relation.
terra: أَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ repeats surah 90’s final designation, confirming that its newly bound people belong to an eschatological company.
terra: أَصْحَابُ الْمَشْأَمَةِ stand opposite the company of the right in 56:8, repeating the boundary between the two human companies at the end of surah 90.

luna: The section explicitly connects q-r-b, nearness, with those drawn near to God; this ayah names them al-muqarrabūn. | terra: The foremost are الْمُقَرَّبُونَ, extending the section’s nearness root from blood relation to the nearness granted by faithful action.
terra: The repeated question about أَصْحَابُ الْيَمِينِ directly restages the final company named in surah 90 and opens the description of their shared reward.

luna: The section's dictionary form tirb means a peer who grows alongside you; this ayah uses atrāban for equal-aged companions, giving the orphan's lost companionship a restored form. | terra: أَتْرَابًا supplies the Quranic occurrence of the section’s secondary ترب sense, people of matching age who belong together rather than a poor person cast into dust.
terra: The question about the companions of the left renews the opposing company just after the companions of the right have been described.
luna: When the dying person is among those brought near, the ayah names rest, provision, and a garden; it extends the section's q-r-b link to a final welcome.
terra: Boasting and rivalry in wealth and children are compared to vegetation that delights and then withers, setting transient offspring-pride against the enduring bond of faith and mercy.
terra: Prophethood and scripture are placed among the descendants of Noah and Abraham, another instance of lineage preserving and transmitting a guiding word.

luna: The ayah says wives are not mothers except those who gave birth to them; it makes actual birth the boundary of the section's womb-based kinship. | terra: The ayah rejects a false maternal claim by saying that mothers are only those who gave birth to them, using وَلَدْنَهُمْ to set the bodily boundary of parenthood.

luna: For the false mother-claim, the expiation is freeing a neck; the ayah connects ruptured kinship language to the section's liberation of a raqaba. | terra: A man retracting words that confused wife with mother must free a neck before the couple touch, placing emancipation beside the guarded boundary between marriage and motherhood.
luna: If a neck cannot be freed, the next expiation is fasting or feeding sixty needy people; this neighbor completes 58:3 by moving from release to feeding.
luna: Faithful people do not take even fathers, sons, brothers, or kin as allies against God; the ayah marks a specific faith boundary within the section's blood ties.
terra: Public wealth is directed to near kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler so that it does not circulate only among the rich, making distribution an instrument of social joining.
terra: Those already settled make room in their hearts for migrants and prefer them despite their own need, a concrete social passage from estrangement and poverty to protected companionship.
terra: Later believers call earlier believers their brothers and ask that no rancor remain in their hearts, extending mercy and attachment across generations.

luna: Kin and children cannot benefit one another on the Day of Resurrection; the section's lineage is real, but faith and mercy determine lasting nearness. | terra: Neither relatives nor children benefit people on the Day of Resurrection, setting a limit on descent as saving nearness and reinforcing 34:37’s correction.
luna: Kindness and justice are permitted toward those who did not fight or expel the believers, extending the section's mercy beyond inherited kin.
terra: Wealth and children can distract believers from remembrance and produce loss, reversing the section’s movement from offspring toward faith and mutual counsel.
luna: Spouses and children can become enemies, yet pardon and forgiveness are urged; family closeness is not automatic, and mercy repairs it.
terra: Wealth and children are a trial, placing a moral boundary around lineage and possession rather than treating either as proof of favor.

luna: A pregnant divorced woman must be supported until delivery; if she nurses the child, she is paid and the parents consult honorably, joining birth to mutual care. | terra: Pregnant women must be housed and maintained until delivery, and nursing is arranged by mutual consultation, turning approaching birth into continued social provision.
luna: The next ayah requires each person to provide according to means, completing 65:6's support for the pregnant mother and child.
terra: Believers must guard themselves and their families from the Fire, turning family attachment into responsibility for the lives that follow them.
luna: The condemned person did not urge feeding the needy, the direct opposite of the section's feeding on a day of hunger and mutual counsel.
luna: No close friend asks after another on that Day; this reverses the section's companion as nearness and protection.

luna: People are made to see one another, completing the scene of estranged companions begun in 70:10. | terra: Although people are made to see one another, the guilty person wishes to ransom himself with his sons, turning the parent-child bond into abandonment under judgment.

luna: A person would ransom his children from the punishment, making offspring a desperate attempted rescue rather than the section's continuing lineage. | terra: The wished-for ransom expands to spouse and brother, adding the closest lateral and marital bonds to the family network sacrificed in 70:11.

luna: He would also ransom his spouse and brother, extending the failure of close bonds in 70:10. | terra: The clan that formerly sheltered the person is also offered as ransom, reversing the section’s sense of kin and companions as protection.
luna: He would ransom everyone on earth to save himself, completing the breakdown of family and clan solidarity.
luna: The righteous reserve a fixed right in their wealth, introducing the next ayah's asker and deprived as recipients of the section's care.
luna: The next ayah names the asker and deprived as holders of that right, specifying the needy person in the section.
terra: God has grown humans from the earth like a growth, giving direct Quranic form to the section’s movement from a lone earthen figure into joined vegetation.
luna: The man God created alone is given wealth and sons; the ayah joins solitude and lineage to a self-satisfied figure like the section's boaster.
luna: The same man has sons at hand, making worldly lineage one of his sources of pride.
luna: His wealth and status are expanded further, completing the description of the man with sons in 74:13.
luna: He still wants more, showing that wealth and descendants do not end self-sufficiency, the stance challenged by the section.

luna: The section ends with aṣḥāb al-maymana, companions of the right; this ayah uses the same companion term for those who escape the Fire. | terra: After 74:38 makes every soul captive to what it earned, this ayah exempts أَصْحَابُ الْيَمِينِ, echoing the section’s move from an unfreed neck to a liberated company of the right.
luna: The question about what brought people to Saqar begins a passage that identifies failure to pray and feed the needy, the section's contrary path.
luna: The condemned say they were not among those who prayed; this is the first failure in the sequence opposing the section's right-hand community.

luna: They say they did not feed the needy, directly reversing the section's relief for the poor. | terra: The condemned confess that they did not feed the needy; beside 74:39, this identifies failure of the section’s feeding and mercy as what separates them from the company of the right.
luna: They joined those who indulged in vain talk, the contrary social company completing the feeding failure in 74:44.
luna: They denied the Day of Judgment; this completes the answer to 74:42 and links the abandoned poor to moral accountability.

luna: The human begins as an emitted drop, directly connecting the section's offspring to bodily origin. | terra: The human begins as a drop of emitted fluid, opening a compact account of the formation that precedes birth.

luna: The drop becomes a clinging clot and is formed, specifying the next stage of 75:37. | terra: The drop becomes a clinging form that God creates and proportions, developing the womb-creation begun in 75:37.

luna: The formed human is made male and female, completing the reproductive sequence begun in 75:37. | terra: God makes from that formed life the male and female pair, completing the passage’s movement from gestation to future parenthood.

luna: The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own desire for the food, bringing the section's three vulnerable figures into one act of mercy. | terra: Food is given despite love for it to the needy, orphan, and captive, closely matching the ascent through feeding and release toward a merciful company.
luna: Humanity is created from a lowly fluid, a direct bodily origin for the section's descendants.
luna: The fluid is placed in a secure resting place, echoing the section's womb as a vessel.
luna: The placement lasts to a known term, giving the section's nearing birth a stated duration.
luna: God measures the term, completing the pregnancy sequence of 77:20-22.

luna: The word atrāban repeats the Qur'anic peer sense of the section's dictionary form tirb, here describing companions of equal age. | terra: أَتْرَابًا again names equal-aged companions, completing the Quran’s repeated evidence for the secondary ترب sense developed by the section.

luna: On that Day a person flees from his brother, a stark reversal of the section's companion and joined-kin images. | terra: On that Day a person flees from his brother, beginning the dissolution of the family network that the section works to bind.

luna: The same person flees from his mother and father, showing descent bonds failing at Judgment. | terra: A person also flees mother and father, reversing the originating parent-child bond of وَالِدٍ وَمَا وَلَدَ.

luna: He flees from his spouse and children, completing the reversal of the section's family and offspring ties. | terra: Flight from spouse and children completes the scene of kinship unable by itself to hold people together at judgment.

luna: The buried girl is asked for what sin she was killed; this is a stark reversal of lineage surviving through birth and of the child whose life does not continue. | terra: The buried infant girl is brought forward and questioned, giving a face to offspring whose life and lineage were violently cut off.

luna: The next ayah says the buried girl was killed; it completes the violated birth and survival implied in 81:8. | terra: The question “for what sin was she killed?” exposes the injustice in 81:8 and makes the destruction of a child answerable before God.
luna: The section names those brought near as a form of q-r-b; this ayah uses al-muqarrabūn for those who witness the record of the righteous.
luna: The same near ones drink from the sealed spring; it repeats the section's q-r-b link between closeness and a valued company.
luna: The human is told to consider what he was created from, turning attention to the body's origin as the section does through birth and descent.
luna: The origin is an emitted fluid, specifying the question in 86:5.
luna: The fluid's bodily source is named, completing the reproductive origin described in 86:6.
luna: The Lord is described as watching over people, completing the warning about oversight before the next passage tests how wealth treats orphan and poor.
luna: The wealthy person assumes abundance means honor; this sets up the section's challenge to the man who boasts of spending heaps.
luna: The person whose provision is narrowed assumes God has humiliated him; this contrasts worldly measurement with the section's care for the poor.

luna: The passage says they do not honor the orphan, directly reversing the section's command to aid the fatherless child. | terra: Failing to honor the orphan is presented as a moral exposure, the opposite response to the severed child whom surah 90 places on the ascent.

luna: They do not urge one another to feed the poor, the exact social failure opposed by the section's feeding and mutual counsel. | terra: The failure to urge one another to feed the needy reverses both the section’s feeding and its reciprocal counsel.
luna: They consume inheritance greedily; this reverses the section's concern for descendants and relatives left after a death.
luna: They love wealth intensely, the opposite of turning wealth toward the orphan and destitute in the section.

luna: God found the Prophet an orphan and sheltered him; the ayah makes the orphan's threatened isolation a scene of received protection. | terra: God finds the Prophet an orphan and gives shelter, the clearest reversal within life of the section’s orphan as one left alone by parental loss.

luna: The instruction not to oppress an orphan turns the Prophet's own orphanhood into a duty of care. | terra: The command not to oppress the orphan turns recognition of parental rupture into the protective conduct demanded by the section.
luna: The asker must not be repelled; it extends the section's mercy from orphan to another person in need.
luna: The ayah says the human was created from a clot, a direct formation-in-the-womb image behind the section's birth arc.
luna: The human transgresses when he sees himself self-sufficient, a precise counterpart to the section's boastful spender who imagines no one sees him.
luna: The self-sufficient person forgets dependence; the section's faith and mercy answer this posture with mutual obligation.
luna: The ayah asks whether the opponent knows that God sees him, a direct formulation of the section's challenge to the man who thinks nobody saw him.

luna: The section names insan and mutual counsel; this preceding ayah declares humankind in loss, which 103:3 then qualifies by faith, good works, truth, and patience. | terra: The human is declared in loss; 103:3 then identifies faith, good action, and reciprocal counsel as the relations that keep a person from remaining isolated in that loss.

luna: The section develops tawāṣaw as joining people through connected counsel; this ayah repeats tawāṣaw for truth and patience, the very communal practice named in 90:17. | terra: Belief and good works are sustained by mutual تَوَاصَوْا to truth and patience, the closest Quranic parallel to the section’s people becoming connected through shared counsel.
luna: The wealth collector thinks his property will make him last forever, a specific contrast to the section's lineage and communal care.
luna: The next ayah says he will be thrown into the Crusher, completing the false security attached to wealth in 104:2.

luna: The Lord of the House feeds against hunger and gives safety from fear, matching the section's hard day of hunger and faith as fear's removal. | terra: God feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them against fear, bringing the feeding of want and the root sense of faith as fear’s removal into one compact pair.
luna: The one who denies judgment is identified through how he treats the orphan, connecting belief to the section's measure of mercy.

luna: The denier pushes away the orphan, a direct reversal of the section's aid to the fatherless. | terra: The denier violently repels the orphan, intensifying the section’s image of a child already severed from a father into deliberate social exclusion.

luna: He does not urge feeding the poor, the opposite of the section's feeding and mutual exhortation. | terra: Not urging the feeding of the needy is the negative counterpart to feeding in surah 90 and mutually binding people through mercy.

luna: God neither begets nor is begotten; the ayah sets a precise divine boundary against the human birth and lineage that opens the section. | terra: لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ reverses both poles of the section’s human oath—begetting and being begotten—to mark the absolute boundary between created lineage and God.
